gate.changed: What the text says: Gita 1.29 (the body fails), 2.7 (teach me), 2.11 (grief for what needs no grief), 2.14 (sensations come and go), 2.62-63 (the eight-link chain), 2.67 (the ship in the storm), 2.47 (the right to work, not the fruit), 2.48 (equanimity is yoga), 2.50 (skill in action), 2.40 (no effort lost), 2.70 (the ocean), 2.58 (the tortoise), 2.56 (the settled mind); Katha Upanishad 1.3.3-4 (the chariot) and Mundaka 3.1.1 (two birds) in our paraphrase.
gate.care: For a viewer who has never opened the Gita and lies awake looping on one thing: what does the oldest Indian text on a mind that will not act say is happening, which part of you let go, and what is the one thing to try tonight?
gate.added: Our reading, marked OUR NOTE throughout: the 2 a.m. loop as grief paid in advance (from 2.11), the weather model of feeling (from 2.14), the chain as an engine with eight gears (from 2.62-63), the chariot as a case board with six parts named one by one, the two-column exercise (from 2.47), the rope and the snake as the verdict (Advaita's classic example).
gate.invalidate: The text is about grief, duty and a battle, not overthinking: 2.11 names the dead and the living, not outcomes; the chariot is from the Katha Upanishad, not the Gita; 2.47 has centuries of competing readings (Shankara, Ramanuja, Gandhi, Tilak) and ours is the plain-sense one; the English on screen is an edited copy of Purohit Swami (1935), not his exact wording; none of this is clinical advice.
gate.monitor: Whether the viewer can do the two columns tonight; the comments for verse-number corrections; chapter three next (why doing nothing is not an option).

sa: योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते

scene.en: Perform all your actions with your mind concentrated on the Divine, renouncing attachment and looking upon success and failure with an equal eye. Spirituality implies equanimity.
